notes.meaning: The heavenly messenger continues speaking to Daniel. He explains that during the first year of King Darius the Mede, he stood by Darius to strengthen and protect him. God used his angel to guide and protect this ruler so that the Jewish captives could be treated well and allowed to return home.

The angel outlines the future rulers of the Persian Empire. Three kings would follow Cyrus—Cambyses, Pseudo-Smerdis, and Darius Hystaspes—before a fourth king, Xerxes, arose with immense wealth. Xerxes used his vast riches and power to launch a massive invasion against Greece.

A powerful warrior-king, Alexander the Great of Greece, would arise and conquer the Persian Empire. He ruled with absolute control and did whatever he pleased across a vast territory. His rapid rise shows how quickly earthly kingdoms can change when God directs history.

At the very peak of his power, Alexander died suddenly, and his vast empire was shattered. Instead of passing down to his children, his realm was broken into four separate kingdoms ruled by his generals. Worldly power is fragile and cannot guarantee a lasting family legacy.

The prophecy narrows its focus to the two kingdoms that surrounded the land of Israel. The king of the South, Ptolemy I of Egypt, would grow powerful, but one of his officers, Seleucus I, would break away and build an even larger empire in the North based in Syria. These two dynasties would constantly battle over the land where God's people lived.

Decades later, the rulers of Egypt and Syria tried to make peace through a royal wedding. The Egyptian princess Berenice married Antiochus II of Syria, but the political alliance quickly collapsed. Antiochus took back his former wife, who then poisoned him and had Berenice, her child, and her attendants murdered.

Berenice's brother, Ptolemy III Euergetes, became king of Egypt and marched out to avenge his sister's murder. He invaded Syria, captured key fortresses belonging to King Seleucus II, and won a series of decisive victories. God's word accurately showed that human violence brings severe consequences.

The victorious Egyptian king carried off vast amounts of gold and silver treasures, along with thousands of captured idols. Among these were sacred Egyptian images that Persian conquerors had carried away long before. After this conquest, he left the northern king alone for several years.
The king of the North tried to strike back by launching an invasion against Egypt. His counterattack completely failed, and he was forced to retreat to his own land empty-handed.

The sons of the northern king prepared for war to reclaim their lost territories. After the older brother died, Antiochus III the Great swept southward like an overflowing river, pushing the Egyptian forces all the way back to their frontier fortress at Raphia.

Furious at this threat to his borders, King Ptolemy IV of Egypt marched out to fight Antiochus III. Although the Syrian king had assembled a massive army, God allowed Antiochus to be soundly defeated, and his large force fell into Egyptian hands.

After slaughtering tens of thousands of Syrian soldiers, the Egyptian king became filled with pride. Instead of pressing his advantage to secure a lasting victory, he returned to a life of luxury and laziness, so his success did not make him truly stronger.

Years later, Antiochus III returned with an even larger army and abundant supplies. Ptolemy IV had died, leaving Egypt under the rule of a young child, which gave the northern king an opportunity to strike back.

Many allies, including Macedonia, joined the Syrian king against Egypt. Factious, violent men among Daniel's own people rebelled against Egyptian rule to help Antiochus, thinking they were fulfilling prophecy and gaining independence, but their revolt collapsed in defeat.

Antiochus III laid siege to the heavily fortified city of Sidon, building dirt ramps against its walls. Even the best Egyptian soldiers and generals could not withstand the attack, and the city was forced to surrender.

Antiochus III conquered without facing any successful resistance and took firm control of Judea, called the Beautiful Land. The Jewish people initially welcomed him, but their land suffered damage and heavy costs as the armies marched through it.

Antiochus planned to take over Egypt through a scheming agreement rather than full-scale war. He gave his daughter Cleopatra in marriage to young Ptolemy V, hoping she would secretly work to destroy Egypt from within. The scheme failed because Cleopatra loved her husband and stayed loyal to him rather than her father.

Antiochus turned his fleet toward the Mediterranean coastlands and islands, capturing many Greek ports. His arrogance soon met its match when the Roman commander Scipio defeated his forces, putting an end to the Syrian king's insults and turning the humiliation back onto him.

Defeated and humiliated by Rome, Antiochus retreated to the strongholds of his own homeland. Desperate to pay the heavy fines Rome demanded, he tried to rob a pagan temple in Elymais and was killed by the outraged local residents.

His son Seleucus IV Philopator took the throne and sent out tax collectors, including an official named Heliodorus, to heavily tax his subjects and plunder the temple in Jerusalem. After a short reign, he was quietly poisoned by his own treasurer rather than dying in battle or in public rebellion.

A despicable ruler, Antiochus IV Epiphanes, then took the throne. He was not the lawful heir, but he came in a time of peace and used flattery, bribes, and political tricks to seize control. His deceitful rise shows how corrupt leaders can gain power through smooth words and scheming.

Large armies were swept away and crushed before Antiochus IV as he expanded his rule. He also removed and murdered the godly high priest Onias III, the prince of the covenant, replacing him with corrupt men who paid for the office.
